A stumble and a permanent fall are two different things, friend. I've tripped over my own mustache more than once, and I'm still standing right here on my gold base.

That's it. Paul asks if they stumbled so as to fall beyond recovery, and his answer is “Certainly not!” So Israel's stumble is not the end of the story. Anybody who has dropped a whole tray of cookies knows you can stumble and still get back to baking.

Yes, salvation. Paul says that because of their trespass, salvation has come to the Gentiles, the people outside Israel. That's good news for every Gentile baker reading this. Salvation is the thing in the box here.

Not this time, friend. Paul doesn't say the law came to the Gentiles in this verse. He says salvation has come to them. When the label says one thing, I don't go grabbing a different ingredient off the shelf.

Jealous is the word. Paul says salvation has come to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous. He comes back to it in verse 14, where he hopes to provoke his own people to jealousy. When Paul says a word twice in four verses, I'm writing it on my apron.

Ashamed sounds like a reasonable guess, but Paul doesn't use it here. The word in the verse is jealous. He says salvation came to the Gentiles to make Israel jealous. I'd feel bad handing you a word Paul never said.

Afraid does show up in this passage, but it's in a different spot. Paul tells the Gentiles, “Do not be arrogant, but be afraid.” (Romans 11:20). Here in verse 11, the word aimed at Israel is jealous. Same letter, different verse, and I've been known to grab the oven mitt when I wanted the spatula.

Same amount would be a flat batch, and Paul isn't baking flat. He says, “…how much greater riches will their fullness bring!” Greater means more than before. If a recipe says double and you make the same, you'll have some very confused cookies.
Yes, save. Paul hopes to provoke his own people to jealousy “…and save some of them.” His hope isn't just to stir them up. He wants them saved. Good teachers always know where they're headed.

Warning is a fair thing to think of, but that isn't Paul's word here. He says he hopes to provoke his own people to jealousy “…and save some of them.” His hope is to see them saved, not just warned. A warning is a flashing timer, and he's after the finished cookie.

Not this verse, friend. Paul hopes to provoke his own people to jealousy “…and save some of them.” He doesn't say judge. He says save, and that tells you where his heart is pointed: toward rescuing them, not sentencing them.

That's what he says. Paul asks, “…what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?” He's already said their rejection is the reconciliation of the world. Then he asks what their acceptance will be, and this is his answer. That's a big finish.

It's a pretty phrase, but it's not what Paul says here. He asks, “…what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?” Life from the dead is his answer. Light to the nations is a nice thought, but it isn't what this verse says.

That sounds lovely, but Paul says something else in this verse. He asks, “…what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?” Those are his exact words about their acceptance. Peace on the earth is a nice cookie, but it's not the one he's baking here.

explanations.answer: The whole batch is holy too
explanations.explanation: Right. Paul says, “If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch…” The first part and the whole batch go together. I've pressed a lot of dough in my day, and I like how Paul used a bakery picture.

explanations.answer: Only that first part is holy
explanations.explanation: Paul goes further than that. He says, “If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch…” The holiness doesn't stop at the first piece. If a batch only counted its first cookie, I'd be out of a job.

explanations.answer: The rest must be made holy
explanations.explanation: That's not what Paul says. He says, “If the first part of the dough is holy, so is the whole batch…” He doesn't talk about the rest needing to be made holy. He just says the whole batch is.

Yes. Paul tells the wild olive shoot, “…do not boast over those branches.” Being grafted in is a gift, so there's nothing to brag about. If I strutted around the counter bragging about my stamping, the cookies would just laugh at me.

Grief isn't what he says here. Paul tells the shoot, “…do not boast over those branches.” Paul himself writes of great sorrow for his own people, Israel (Romans 9:2 and 3), but that's a different spot in the letter. In this verse the warning is about boasting.
Worry isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says, “…do not boast over those branches.” That's the instruction he gives. Worrying is a different thing, and I'd save it for when the oven is acting up.

Yes, that's true. Paul says, “You do not support the root, but the root supports you.” The wild shoot doesn't hold the tree up. It's the other way around. Any branch that starts thinking it's carrying the trunk needs a little lie-down.

It's true, and Paul says it plainly. His words are, “You do not support the root, but the root supports you.” So the grafted-in shoot isn't the one supporting the root. The root is supporting the shoot. I'd say that's good news for any branch.

Works is a common guess, but it's not what Paul says. He says, “…but you stand by faith.” Faith is the word that goes in the blank. Unbelief is why the natural branches were broken off, and faith is how the shoot stands.
Not in this verse, friend. Paul says the natural branches were broken off because of unbelief, “…but you stand by faith.” The law isn't what the shoot stands by here. Faith is.

It's actually true. Paul says, “And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.” So for those branches, grafting back in is on the table. That's good news, and I'd hold onto it.

explanations.answer: They'll be grafted in more readily
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. Paul writes, “…how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!” If a wild shoot can be grafted in, the natural ones belong there even more. It's their own tree, after all.

explanations.answer: They'll be grafted in more slowly
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. He writes, “…how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!” Readily means more easily, not less. If a wild shoot can be grafted in, the natural ones fit their own tree even better.

explanations.answer: They'll need a different olive tree
explanations.explanation: Paul says it's their own olive tree. He writes, “…how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!” So no new tree is needed. They're going back where they started.
